indomitable

in-DOM-ih-tuh-bul -- Latin in- ('not') + domitare ('to tame'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Indomitable is impossible to subdue, defeat, or discourage.

The small fishing village's indomitable spirit kept it rebuilding after every single hurricane season.

Example

Even after being voted out of student council twice, she ran again the following year with the same indomitable determination.

That refusal to be discouraged or defeated, no matter how many setbacks pile up, is exactly what indomitable describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unstoppable: Unstoppable means impossible to halt once in motion — an unstoppable rally, an unstoppable rise. Indomitable is about spirit rather than momentum: an indomitable person can be stopped, beaten, even flattened, and still refuses to stay discouraged. Unstoppable describes the progress; indomitable describes the will underneath it.

unflinching: Unflinching means facing something frightening or painful without pulling back — an unflinching gaze, an unflinching report. Indomitable goes beyond one hard moment: an indomitable spirit keeps refusing defeat through setback after setback. Unflinching is steadiness in a single moment; indomitable is a will nothing can subdue.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

yielding: giving in easily to pressure

fainthearted: lacking courage or resolve

Where it sits · how completely it withstands every attack

unyielding → indomitable → unconquerable

unyielding vs. indomitable: Unyielding is milder than indomitable: an unyielding negotiator refuses to budge on one price, while an indomitable spirit cannot be subdued or discouraged by anything at all.

unconquerable vs. indomitable: Unconquerable is stronger than indomitable: an indomitable defender refuses to be discouraged, but an unconquerable fortress goes further — in centuries its walls were never once breached.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-: not (Latin)

root — -domit-: to tame, master (Latin (domare))

suffix — -able: able to be, capable of being (Latin (-abilis))

Put it together: Latin in- ('not') plus domare ('to tame') plus -able ('able to be') -- indomitable literally means 'not able to be tamed' or mastered.

Use the root in a new word: dominate: The home team began to dominate the second half, scoring three unanswered goals.

Word Building

Word Choice

Indomitable almost always describes a spirit, will, or determination that survives real hardship -- it's a strong, admiring word, rarely used sarcastically.
